activities.anchor: Every phone, laptop, server and smart washing machine is this design
activities.caption: bet before you read on — it is 1944, new program required
activities.name: archStoredPredict

config.q: It is 1944. The computer has finished one calculation and must start a completely different program. What happens next?
choices: Crews rewire the circuits for days — the program is the wiring
New instructions are loaded into the same memory that holds the data
A fresh deck of cards replaces the processor's settings
The results are printed, and the next user re-solders the arithmetic unit
config.why: Until the stored-program concept (the 1945 report), the program WAS the wiring; after it, instructions live in the same memory as the data, in the same binary language, and changing the task means loading them.

activities.anchor: shop assistants say it and the box is the biggest thing in sight
activities.caption: find the faulty line — what is actually inside the case
activities.name: archBoxSpot

config.prompt: One of these claims about a desktop setup is wrong — click it:
lines: The whole case under the desk is 'the CPU'.
A CPU is a single chip a few centimetres across.
The case also holds memory, storage, power supply, cooling and ports.
A phone carries several cores on one chip — and has no desktop case at all.
Memory is the desk surface; storage is the filing cabinet down the hall.
config.correction: The case is the building; the CPU is one hyperactive office worker inside it — a chip a few centimetres across.
config.why: The case-equals-CPU confusion evaporates the moment you notice a whole computer fits behind a sheet of glass.

activities.anchor: and the names matter because the exam asks for them
activities.caption: pair each register and unit with its one job
activities.name: archRegsMatch

config.prompt: Pair each part of the CPU with its single job:

pairs.right: the mathematics and the comparisons — addition, AND, OR, shifts, tests for zero
decodes instructions and sends the control signals that tell memory, ALU and devices what to do, and when
holds the address of the next instruction
holds the address currently being read from or written to

config.why: Five named parts, five single jobs — the register list is a cast list, not a vocabulary drill.

activities.anchor: The three stages and their traffic are worth walking slowly
activities.caption: walk the loop — what moves, when
activities.name: archFdeOrder

config.prompt: One pass of the cycle, in order:
items: The program counter holds the address of the next instruction; the address travels down the address bus.
Memory sends the instruction back along the data bus to the memory data register.
The instruction moves to the current instruction register — and the counter is incremented during fetch, before the work starts.
The control unit decodes the operation code and works out what must be done.
Execute: the ALU computes, a value is written, or a device acts — then the loop repeats, billions of times each second.
config.why: Fetch, decode, execute — and the counter already points onward, which is how the processor knows where to go next without being told.

activities.anchor: a recipe card nailed to the wall and a clearable worktop
activities.caption: file each fact by the memory tier it describes
activities.name: archMemSort

config.prompt: Three tiers of memory, three roles — file each fact:

items.label: volatile — the power cut, the contents gone
holds the startup firmware the processor runs the instant power arrives
fast, read-write workspace where running programs and unsaved edits live
a few megabytes at most, only read in ordinary operation
large, permanent filing — read-write and non-volatile, but a different device entirely
pulling the plug destroys it instantly — yet the machine still boots afterwards

config.why: ROM remembers but is fixed; RAM is fast but forgets; the drive holds everything while the power is off.

activities.name: archDevicesCloze

config.text: A 2D scanner sweeps light across a page and records the %%0%% with an array of light sensors; with %%1%% software the resulting image becomes editable text. Inkjet printers fire microscopic %%2%% of liquid ink directly onto the page; 3D printers build a physical object one %%3%% at a time from melted filament.

activities.anchor: Optical discs are cheap and portable, and useful for distribution
activities.caption: call the size of one Blu-ray layer
activities.name: archBlurayEst

config.prompt: A single layer of Blu-ray storage — pits read by a blue-violet laser — holds roughly how much?
config.why: 25 GB per layer: the finer the laser's wavelength, the smaller the pits — infrared gave CD about 700 MB, red gave DVD 4.7 GB per layer.
config.context: Three decades of finer light: 700 MB → 4.7 GB → 25 GB, one layer at a time.

activities.anchor: my machine slowed down, so I need more gigabytes
activities.caption: the sluggish desktop — walk the diagnosis
activities.name: archSlowBranch

config.root: The family desktop has been feeling sluggish. Walk the diagnosis.

start.text: The complaint: everything takes ages to open.

choices.label: Buy the biggest storage on sale — size must be the problem
choices.feedback: Capacity and speed are separate axes: a 4 TB HDD is far slower than a 256 GB SSD in practice.

choices.label: Find out what the processor is waiting on
choices.feedback: Often the true bottleneck: the processor sits idle while storage trickles data across.

wait.text: Storage is an old mechanical disk with millisecond access; RAM is nearly full.

choices.label: Fit an SSD for the operating system and programs
choices.feedback: Dozens of times quicker at typical tasks — boots in seconds, programs open instantly.

choices.label: Add RAM, so less data swaps between memory and disk
choices.feedback: Extra workspace means fewer swaps — the other honest fix.

capTrap.text: Two identical laptops, one with a 2 TB HDD and one with a 512 GB SSD — the smaller boots in seconds, the larger takes minutes, because it is mechanical, not because it is small.

ssdFix.text: Boots in seconds, opens instantly — the speed axis, not the capacity axis, decided the last decade of hardware.

ramFix.text: Less swapping, less waiting — the desktop feels new again.

config.why: Slowness usually means the processor is waiting on storage — the honest fix is a quicker device or extra memory, never just room to fill.
